title_en: Documenting Room Condition at Handover: A Landlord's Protection
summary_en: Why a timestamped photo record at move-in is a landlord's best protection in a deposit dispute.
body_en:
Most deposit disputes aren't really about money. They're about two different memories of what the room looked like on day one. A simple photo record settles that argument before it starts, and takes less time than the dispute itself.

What to photograph before the tenant moves in

  • Every wall, the floor, and the ceiling, especially any existing marks, cracks or stains.
  • The mattress, wardrobe interior, aircon unit, and window — the items most likely to show wear over time.
  • Light switches, power points, and the door lock, to prove they were working at handover.
  • Any furniture you're providing, such as a wardrobe or desk, from more than one angle.

How to make the record actually useful later

  • Send the photos directly to your tenant on the same day, through the same chat you'll use for the tenancy. This gives both of you a dated, shared record.
  • Ask your tenant to confirm they've seen the photos and agree the room matches them — a simple message confirming the room matches is enough.
  • Keep the photos somewhere you can find them months later, not just in a chat you might lose access to.
  • Note the date on each photo set, either in the filename or in the message you send with it.

Do the same thing at move-out

Repeat the same photos when the tenant leaves, from the same angles if you can. Comparing the two sets side by side makes any real damage obvious, and makes a fair deposit deduction easy to explain.

Why this protects you specifically

Without a dated record, a deposit disagreement often comes down to whose word is trusted more. A photo record removes that guesswork, and it protects an honest tenant just as much as it protects you — which tends to make the whole tenancy feel more trustworthy from day one.
